endorsements.quote: Second, it should be noted that any documentation (audio or video) of clinical conversations would necessarily require the patient’s full awareness, based on clear and comprehensive information, and explicit, documented consent.

Even if AI is framed as “decision support,” its use in end-of-life contexts still requires explicit governance—clear lines of accountability, auditability, and oversight—so that responsibility is not implicitly shifted from clinicians and institutions onto an opaque system.

unlisted_practices: Reserve training of large-scale AI models for clinical problems that cannot be adequately addressed through less energy-intensive approaches.
Do not use AI to reconstruct the presumed end-of-life wishes of incapacitated patients from recorded clinical conversations or digital footprints in its current form.
Evaluate whether AI tools support rather than undermine the care relationship between clinicians and patients before adoption.
Clinicians should engage in developing AI tools designed to support the care relationship and aligned with fundamental values and rights.

screen.reason: This is a position paper/editorial from the SIAARTI Ethics Committee discussing ethical concerns and governance requirements for using AI in end-of-life decision-making.
